title: The Car Division Kiichiro Toyoda Started Inside a Loom Works
dek: In September 1933 Kiichiro Toyoda began building cars inside a textile-machinery company that doubted him, and its first trucks broke down on the road.

story.company: Toyoda Automatic Loom Works (later Toyota Motor Co.)
story.event: Setting up an automotive division inside the family loom company
story.summary: On 1 September 1933 Kiichiro Toyoda set up an automotive production division inside Toyoda Automatic Loom Works in Kariya, despite opposition over the capital it would need and a Japanese market dominated by Ford and General Motors assembly plants. Shareholders tripled the company's capital in January 1934; the first G1 truck prototype, finished in August 1935, broke down on early runs, and in 1937 the division became Toyota Motor Co.
paragraphs: On 1 September 1933, Kiichiro Toyoda set up an automotive production division inside Toyoda Automatic Loom Works, the family's textile-machinery company in Kariya. Toyota's own history points out the date: ten years earlier, on the day of the Great Kanto earthquake, he had been in Tokyo to talk about cars with a friend. The new division was not yet formally part of the company. Its members were engineers who had been studying engines with him between jobs on looms.

He knew the odds. Ford had assembled imported kits in Yokohama since 1925 and General Motors in Osaka since 1927, and his friend wrote that the two all but monopolised car sales in Japan. Hakuyosha, a Japanese maker that built about 230 cars, had closed. Many inside and outside the loom works opposed the venture because of the capital it needed, and the president, Risaburo Toyoda, saw it as risky. Kiichiro argued that the company had the technical skill, sound finances after its recovery from the depression, and a government preparing to support domestic carmakers.

He started small. His team had copied bought engines to make ten small ones, and in October 1933 they took apart a new Chevrolet. He designed around parts that fitted the Fords and Chevrolets already on Japanese roads, so owners could find spares. On 29 January 1934 shareholders tripled the capital to three million yen and added motors and powered transport to the company's purposes. One account says his late father, Sakichi, gave him the whole £100,000 from selling loom patents to Platt Brothers of England; Toyota's history records that Platt eventually paid £83,500.

The first results were rough. At the government's request the company turned to trucks, and the first G1 prototype was finished on 25 August 1935. On a test run that September a rear-axle weld broke; in November the steering failed on the way to its Tokyo presentation, and repairs delayed it until 4 a.m. the next day. Kiichiro later wrote that the first vehicles shipped "were hardly usable by today's standards." In 1936 the government licensed the loom works as a carmaker, and in 1937 the division became Toyota Motor Co., with Risaburo as president and Kiichiro as vice-president.

quote.text: Next in the contest, you must be covered with sand, sometimes dislocate a hand, sprain an ankle, swallow a quantity of dust, be scourged with the whip; and after undergoing all this, you must sometimes be conquered.
quote.locator: Discourses, Book III, Chapter XV, "That we ought to proceed with circumspection to everything"
quote.source_title: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus with the Encheiridion, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #10661
quote.connection: Epictetus tells a would-be Olympic champion to count the dust, the sprains and the whip, and then defeat as well. Kiichiro counted for years and still watched his first trucks break on the road. Careful reckoning did not spare him the losses; it only meant he had agreed to them in advance.

reflection: Kiichiro did not leave the loom works to build cars. He started a division that was not yet on the organisation chart, copied engines, took a Chevrolet apart, and asked shareholders for money once there was something to show. Even so, his first trucks broke down on the way to their own launch.

It is tempting to believe that enough preparation will spare you the embarrassing first version. It rarely does. What preparation buys is the ability to take the failure without stopping: people who can repair an axle overnight, and a plan that expected some breakage. It helps to decide in advance which failures you will treat as ordinary.
invitation: Think of the next piece of work you will show someone. Write down the one part most likely to break in front of them, and decide now what you will say if it does.

cross_checks.claim: The automotive division was set up inside Toyoda Automatic Loom Works on 1 September 1933.
The venture faced opposition over the capital it needed, Risaburo Toyoda saw it as risky, and Kiichiro persuaded him to proceed.
In 1933 the team took apart a new Chevrolet to learn from it.
In 1934 shareholders raised the capital to three million yen and added automobile manufacture to the company's purposes.
In 1936 the loom works was licensed as one of Japan's carmakers.
In 1937 the division became Toyota Motor Co., with Risaburo as president and Kiichiro as vice-president.

research_notes: Platt money: the International Directory of Company Histories (via Encyclopedia.com) says Sakichi sold the loom patents to Platt Brothers for £100,000 and gave the whole sum to Kiichiro for car research; Toyota's own 75-year history gives the agreed price as £100,000 in four annual instalments but says the unpaid balance was cut in July 1934, so Platt paid £83,500 in total, and it does not link the payments to car research. The story gives the popular account as 'one account' and Toyota's figure beside it, and does not say the money paid for the cars. Who needed persuading: some secondary accounts (for example Wikipedia) say Kiichiro persuaded his father, but Sakichi died in 1930; the Toyota Commemorative Museum says he persuaded the company president, Risaburo Toyoda, and the story follows the museum. Capital: Toyota dates the tripling to the extraordinary shareholders meeting of 29 January 1934 (one to three million yen); the museum's Kiichiro chronology and the International Directory record a further doubling at a 1935 meeting, which the story does not use. The 1 September link to the 1923 earthquake comes from Toyota's history and is attributed to it. Kiichiro's 'hardly usable' remark is from the prospectus for Toyota Motor Co. as translated on Toyota's site; 'today's standards' therefore means those of about 1937. The friend's monopoly remark (Hideo Kobayashi) is paraphrased, not quoted. Toyota's history describes the 1936 designation as provisional, so the story says only that the government licensed the loom works. The Epictetus passage is advice to someone who wants to win at the Olympic games; it is applied here by analogy.
